criterion_notes.c1: The article thematically addresses household, community, school and health-care facility water, sanitation and hygiene (WASH) service access and associated monitoring indicators (e.g. on-premises water, collection time, open defecation and shared sanitation).
criterion_notes.c2: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the fourth priority area briefly mentions women's participation in local WASH governance bodies and water committees as a measurement gap, though only in passing commentary rather than examining how an institutional or governance factor shapes access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is clearly not met (no): the paper does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, eligibility, documentation/tenure, tariff/cost-recovery, enforcement or utility-structure mechanism directly governing service access. Note that even if Criterion 2 were generously treated as met under the plain wording, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude because the article contains no empirical evidence (Criterion 3).
criterion_notes.c3: Published in the 'Perspectives' section of the Bulletin of the World Health Organization, this 3-page article offers a narrative commentary and critique of gender-related WASH indicators based on expert input and non-systematic literature discussion. It contains no primary empirical data, no empirical methods and no systematic empirical synthesis, requiring exclusion under E05.
criterion_notes.c4: No primary or systematically synthesized empirical outcomes on access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability or exclusion are reported; the paper critiques existing survey/SDG indicators and summarizes selected prior studies narratively to identify future research needs.
criterion_notes.c5: Because this is a non-empirical Perspectives commentary, there is no identifiable empirical study population, unit of analysis, exposure, outcome measure or empirical study design.
criterion_notes.c6: The full text is in English, an eligible language without translation.

evidence_quotes.quote: Globally, however, 2.1 billion people do not have access to safe drinking water at home, 2.3 billion do not have basic sanitation
Within each priority area, we describe and critique the status of these measures and identify where further research is needed
The standard water indicators are whether households had sufficient water to meet needs during the past month and how many months out of the year water is available at the main water source.

However, measures of women’s participation in the governance and household decision-making control over such resources is scarce, although such participation may result in more gendered considerations in addressing some of the mentioned issues related to access and safety.
We emphasize the need for measurement at the intersection of gender equality and water, sanitation and hygiene to guide SDG monitoring and achievement.

raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). This 3-page 'Perspectives' article in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization (Kayser et al., 2019) is a narrative commentary critiquing current WASH gender-equality and empowerment monitoring indicators across four priority areas and proposing future research directions. It presents no primary empirical data, no empirical methodology and no systematic review synthesis, and it also does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative or regulatory mechanism governing WASH service access under Criterion 2.
